summary: Describes the Finger protocol, a simple way to ask a remote computer for information about its users. It is based on RFC 742 and clarifies how the two ends should talk without breaking existing implementations. It was replaced by RFC 1196 and later RFC 1288.

eli5.summary: You knock on a computer's door and ask who is home and what they are up to. This describes how to ask politely.

questions: what is the finger security risk
subtitle: A simple protocol to ask a remote host about its users.

tldr.problem: System administrators and users want to check who is logged in and what they are doing on remote systems, but there was no standard way to ask for this information.
tldr.mechanism: Finger is a simple TCP protocol on port 79. A client opens a connection, sends a query line (a username, or empty for all users), and the server responds with user information in plain text before closing.
tldr.outcome: Finger became widely deployed and widely hated due to severe security issues. It was later replaced by RFC 1196 and RFC 1288, but the core protocol remained the same. Today it is rarely used except for nostalgia.

facts.label: Connection
facts.value: Client initiates, server responds, connection closes

today: RFC 1194 was replaced by RFC 1196 and later RFC 1288, which tightened security recommendations. However, the protocol remained fundamentally the same. Today Finger is rarely used except for historical or nostalgia reasons, as modern systems have better directory and presence protocols. The core security issues identified in this RFC—information disclosure, firewall evasion, and implementation attacks—remain relevant to modern protocol design.

sections.title: What Finger Does
sections.content:
Finger is a simple protocol that lets you query a remote computer to find out information about its users. You open a TCP connection to the remote host on port 79, send a one-line query, and receive a human-readable text response with information about that user or all logged-in users.

This RFC clarifies and updates the original Finger protocol (RFC 742) to document how most implementations actually work, especially the popular BSD UNIX version. It tries to avoid breaking existing implementations while defining the expected behavior of both client and server.
sections.eli5: Finger is like a phone call to a computer: you dial the number (TCP port 79), ask a question (who is logged in?), get an answer, and hang up. Anyone on the internet can call, which is both useful and risky.

sections.title: How Queries and Responses Work
sections.content:
A Finger query is a single line of text ending in CRLF (carriage return and line feed). There are three main query types:

  • Empty query ({C}): Request a list of all users currently logged in. The response must include at least each user's full name.
  • Username query ({U}{C}): Request detailed information about a specific user, including office, phone number, login time, and optionally a user-written plan file (like a status message).
  • Forwarding query ({U}{H}{C}): Forward a query to another host. For example, user@host1@host2 asks the server to look up user@host1 and forward the response back. This allows querying users on machines you cannot reach directly.

The server's response is free-form text meant for human reading, not machine parsing. It is generated by a Remote User Information Program (RUIP) running on the remote host. All data must be ASCII (no extended characters or binary), and responses are transmitted plainly before the connection closes.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of questions you can ask: 'who is logged in?', 'tell me about this person', and 'ask another computer about this person for me'. Answers come back as plain English text that a person can read.

sections.title: Security Dangers
sections.content:
The Finger RFC devotes an entire section to security because the protocol presents serious risks. Finger discloses information about users, which is inherently sensitive. The RFC highlights many concerns:

  • User enumeration: An attacker can discover valid usernames by querying the system.
  • Information disclosure: Responses can reveal login times, mail status, idle time, office locations and phone numbers—enough to track a person's activity.
  • Forwarding abuse: The {Q2} forwarding feature can be used to access internal systems through firewalls.
  • User plan files: If servers allow users to write plan files, this becomes an arbitrary information disclosure vulnerability.
  • Execution of user programs: Some implementations allow Finger to run user-specified programs, which is dangerous.
  • Implementation attacks: Malformed Finger queries can exploit bugs in server implementations, especially on security-critical systems.

The RFC strongly recommends that administrators disable forwarding ({Q2}) by default, carefully control what information is returned, filter data in clients to prevent VT100 escape code attacks, and log all Finger queries for audit purposes.
sections.eli5: Finger is like leaving a directory in your front window showing everyone's schedule and office phone numbers. An attacker can learn who works there, when they are usually at their desk, and can possibly break through firewalls by asking one computer to relay queries to another.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
An empty query returns a list of all logged-in users with basic information:

Login Name TTY Idle When Office

A username query returns detailed information for one user, including home directory, shell, last login time, and plan file contents.

A forwarding query like user@host1@host2 asks host2 to contact host1 and return the result. This allows finding users on internal systems from the internet—which is why it is a security risk.
sections.eli5: Asking 'who is online?' gives you a list. Asking about 'Bob' gives you Bob's office, phone, and whatever Bob wrote in his status file. Asking 'Bob@company@branch' asks the company to look up Bob at the branch office and tell you.
